title: What Happens When a Team Member Leaves and Takes Clients? | Adams Cameron
metaDesc: Listings sit with the brokerage, not the team. But relationships walk, and the paperwork almost never decides what actually happens next.
h1: What Happens When a Team Member Leaves and Takes Clients?
about: What a Florida team leader should expect when a team member departs, including what happens to listings and pending transactions, what genuinely travels with a person, and how to prepare in advance
answer: Less dramatically than team leaders fear and more than the paperwork suggests. Listing agreements are with the brokerage rather than with the team or the individual, so the listings themselves do not simply leave, and if the departing agent stays at the same firm the transactions are usually reassigned internally. What genuinely walks out is the relationships, because a past client who worked with that person will call that person. Documents set the boundaries for pending files and money. They do not decide who a client rings next year, and mistaking one for the other is where team leaders go wrong.
takeaways: Listings belong to the brokerage, not to the team or the individual, so pending business does not simply leave with them.
Relationships do leave, and no agreement prevents a past client calling someone they liked.
Settle pending-file compensation in writing before anyone joins, because afterwards it becomes a negotiation under pressure.
Non-compete and non-solicitation terms have real limits in Florida and are worth proper legal advice rather than assumption.
Most departures are ordinary ambition. Treating one as betrayal costs you the referrals that would otherwise have followed.
tldr: When someone leaves a team, the transactions are generally safe because listing agreements sit with the brokerage. The relationships are not, and nothing can make them safe. The practical protections are all in advance: define in writing who gets paid what on pending files, be clear about which clients came from team lead generation and which the individual brought, and take proper advice on any restrictive terms rather than assuming a template works. How the departure is handled usually determines whether the person becomes a referral source or a competitor.
body:
Every team leader eventually gets the conversation, and most handle the first one badly. It is worth thinking through before it happens rather than during.

What does not leave: the transactions

Start with the reassuring part, because it is the thing people panic about first.

A listing agreement is between the seller and the brokerage. Not the team, and not the individual agent who signed it up. The same is true of buyer representation. So when a team member departs, the pending business does not travel with them automatically, and if they are moving within the same brokerage those files are generally reassigned internally so the clients continue to be served.

That is the same structural fact that surprises agents in other situations, covered in what happens if your brokerage is sold and how portable your book of business is. If the person is leaving the firm entirely rather than just the team, the mechanics of pending files and commission are the ones in what happens to your commission on pending deals when you leave a brokerage.

What does leave: the relationships, and nothing stops that

Here is the part no document solves.

A buyer who spent four months in a car with your team member, at weekends, being talked through the worst moments of a purchase, has a relationship with that person. When they sell in six years, they will call that person. They will not call the team name, and they will not consult an agreement.

This is worth accepting rather than fighting, because the alternative is spending money on legal instruments that will not change the outcome and will make you look worse. The relationship followed the human being, which is exactly what you were paying that person to build.

Where it actually gets contentious: the money on pending files

The genuine disputes are almost never about future clients. They are about deals already in progress and who gets paid what.

A team member has a listing under contract that closes six weeks after they leave. They sourced it, they serviced it, and somebody else will handle the closing. What are they owed? Everyone has a strong intuition, the intuitions differ, and if it is not written down the argument is unpleasant and unresolvable.

So write it down before anyone joins. Specifically:

  • What happens to a pending file at departure: does it stay with the team, follow the person, or transfer with a reduced share?
  • What percentage is paid on a deal under contract at departure, and does it change depending on how far along the file is?
  • Who services it after they go, and is that reflected in the split?
  • How and when payment happens, given the closing may be months later.

That belongs in the same conversation as splitting commission fairly with team members, and it should be settled at the point described in setting expectations with new team members from day one. An agreement written while everyone is optimistic is worth ten negotiated while somebody is leaving.

The distinction that decides whether a departure feels fair

Be explicit, from the beginning, about which clients came from where.

A lead generated and paid for by the team, handed to a member to service, is a different thing from a client that person brought from their own network. Teams that never draw that line have the worst departures, because both sides genuinely believe they are owed the relationship and neither is obviously wrong.

Drawing it early does not stop anyone leaving. It does mean that when they do, everyone already agrees on what happened, which is most of what makes a departure civil.

Restrictive terms, and their real limits

Team leaders often want a non-compete or a non-solicitation clause. Both are worth understanding properly rather than assuming a downloaded template does the job.

Restrictive covenants have real limits in Florida and get tested on their reasonableness in scope, duration and geography. A clause that would effectively stop a licensee working in their own market is a different proposition from a narrow agreement about actively soliciting specific clients for a defined period. This is genuinely a matter for a lawyer, and the general treatment of the adjacent question is in whether non-compete clauses hold up when you switch brokerages in Florida.

The practical caution is that even an enforceable clause does not stop a past client picking up the phone unprompted, which is how most of this actually happens.

Handle the departure well, because you are being watched

Two audiences are paying close attention: your remaining team members, and the local market.

If you handle a departure with grace, pay what was agreed promptly, and speak well of the person, your remaining people learn that leaving is survivable and that you are fair. That makes them more likely to stay, not less. If you handle it badly, everyone concludes that they should plan their own exit quietly, which is precisely the culture that produces sudden departures.

The market is small. In a two county footprint you will be across the table from this person, and so will your team. An agent who left on good terms sends referrals for years; one who left badly tells the story for just as long.

Why people actually leave, which is usually not betrayal

Most departures are ambition rather than grievance. Someone has learned the job, wants to keep more of what they produce, wants their own name on the sign, or has discovered they prefer working alone. Those are all reasonable and none of them is about you.

The failure modes that do belong to the team leader are worth reading honestly in what makes a real estate team fail: unclear splits, promised leads that never materialize, and no visible path beyond the current arrangement. If people leave for those reasons, the departure is information rather than an accident.

The honest bottom line

The transactions are safer than you fear and the relationships are less protectable than you hope. Everything that can be controlled is controlled in advance: written terms on pending files, an explicit distinction between team-generated and personally-sourced clients, and proper advice on any restrictive terms.

Beyond that, the variable is how you behave on the way out, which decides whether the person becomes a referral partner or a competitor with a story.

faq.q: Can a departing team member take listings with them?
faq.a: Not automatically. A listing agreement is between the seller and the brokerage rather than the team or the individual, so the listings do not travel with a person. If they are moving within the same brokerage, pending files are generally reassigned internally so the clients continue to be served.

faq.q: Can you stop a former team member contacting past clients?
faq.a: Not in any practical sense. A client who worked closely with that person has a relationship with them and will call them, without consulting any agreement. Restrictive terms have real limits in Florida and are tested on reasonableness, and even an enforceable clause does not stop a past client picking up the phone unprompted.

faq.q: What causes the actual disputes when someone leaves a team?
faq.a: Almost always money on pending files rather than future clients. A deal under contract at departure, sourced and serviced by the person leaving but closed by somebody else, produces strong and conflicting intuitions about what is owed. If it is not written down in advance, the argument is unpleasant and unresolvable.

faq.q: How do you prevent a bad departure?
faq.a: Settle it in writing before anyone joins: what happens to pending files, what percentage is paid on a deal under contract, who services it afterwards and when payment happens. Also be explicit from the start about which clients came from team lead generation and which the individual brought, since teams that never draw that line have the worst departures.

faq.q: Should a team leader use a non-compete?
faq.a: Take proper legal advice rather than assuming a template works. Restrictive covenants are tested on reasonableness in scope, duration and geography, and a clause that would effectively prevent a licensee working in their own market is a very different proposition from a narrow, time-limited agreement about actively soliciting specific clients.

ctaHeading: Write the terms while everyone is still optimistic.
